task.goal: Reduce mislabeled samples in a small soil-testing lab during handoffs.
hard_constraints: Two technicians process 40 samples daily with printed labels and one shared spreadsheet; no barcode purchase.
Original samples and identifiers must remain traceable; do not relabel from memory.
Measure wrong labels, handoff time and unresolved mismatches over two weeks.
task.available_resources: Existing intake forms and last month's correction log.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Source-checked handoff with explicit acceptance
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make each transfer a short, two-person verification. The sender presents the sample and its intake form; the receiver independently reads the identifier on the sample and compares it with the form and the corresponding spreadsheet row before accepting custody. This changes the handoff from an assumed transfer into an explicit check against the original record, potentially catching transpositions and transfers to the wrong row.

Add columns to the shared spreadsheet for sender, receiver, transfer time and status: accepted or mismatch pending. Only one technician edits the transfer record at a time. For a mismatch, retain the sample, existing label and intake form together in a designated hold area. Record the conflicting identifiers verbatim. Resolve using documentary evidence; preserve the original entry and append any correction, its evidence, date and technician. Never replace an identifier from memory.

Use last month's correction log to select the most error-prone handoff for the first trial. The procedure needs no new equipment, but both technicians must overlap briefly at that handoff. It assumes the intake form is a reliable reference; matching errors already present on both form and label may escape detection. The additional coordination could also outweigh the benefit if errors mainly originate elsewhere. Reversal consists of removing the acceptance requirement while retaining all traceability records.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Across two weeks, alternate ordinary and verified handoffs by predetermined half-days, balancing morning and afternoon periods. Keep mismatch containment and measurement identical in both conditions. Record confirmed wrong-label events per sample, elapsed handoff seconds and unresolved mismatches at each day's end, including their age. Apply the same end-of-batch source audit to both conditions and count each error once. Inspect a few transfers first to confirm that the receiver actually checks the source independently. The mechanism is challenged if checks are routinely skipped, wrong-label rates do not improve, or delay and unresolved work increase substantially. With only 40 samples daily, report counts and uncertainty rather than claiming proof.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Fixed-position custody with a traveling manifest
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Keep samples in numbered positions within an existing rack, tray or clearly marked bench area, and hand over the entire group with a position manifest. Each position maps to an original sample identifier copied from the intake form and checked against the printed sample label before loading. The primary mechanism is physical separation and stable placement: technicians need fewer loose-sample transfers in which labels, forms or neighboring samples can become confused.

Record batch, position, original identifier, current custodian and exceptions in a separate spreadsheet tab. A position number is only a location reference, never a replacement sample identifier. Keep each existing sample label intact and retain the intake forms with the batch. At handoff, the receiver checks occupied positions, vacancies and manifest agreement before accepting the group. If processing requires removal, mark the position out; return the sample only after checking its original identifier. Hold unexplained discrepancies without guessing or silently moving samples to make the manifest fit.

Use the correction log to identify whether swaps between neighboring samples or lost batch membership are plausible targets. Prerequisites are sufficient existing space and a workflow that permits samples to stay in assigned positions through at least one handoff. This may offer little benefit where samples must constantly change containers or where labels are already wrong at intake. Positions can also create false confidence, so the manifest cannot substitute for checking identifiers. The procedure is reversible by retiring the location mapping after all samples are reconciled.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For two weeks, allocate comparable batches by a predetermined alternating sequence to fixed-position handling or current handling. Record confirmed wrong labels, handoff duration and daily unresolved mismatch counts and ages for both. Use the same source audit after handoff in both groups. Before live use, conduct a paper-only rehearsal with an intentionally incorrect manifest position; check whether the receiver detects it without relying on location alone. No live sample is deliberately mislabeled. Reject or revise the approach if position records frequently become stale, swaps persist, or maintaining the manifest takes longer than the transfer errors it prevents justify. Interpret low error counts cautiously.

DIRECT_FULL.title: One-sample labeling gate before transfer
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Prevent labels from being assigned to the wrong sample by allowing only one sample, its intake form and its matching printed label in the active labeling area at a time. Complete that sample's label application and source check before bringing the next sample into the area. Keep unused printed labels separate from completed samples. The primary mechanism is reducing opportunities for cross-assignment during preparation, before a handoff exposes the mistake.

Review last month's correction log to identify the step where labels are first applied or a labeled derivative is created. Introduce the gate there. Add spreadsheet fields for source identifier, labeling completion and next custodian. Check the printed identifier against the intake form and the sample's existing identifier before marking completion. For derivatives, record the parent identifier and retain the parent-to-derivative relationship. Never cover or discard an original identifier to make a discrepancy disappear. Isolate unexpected or duplicate labels, preserve the conflicting evidence and append documented corrections rather than overwriting history.

The receiving technician accepts only samples marked complete and checks that each physical sample has a corresponding spreadsheet entry. This requires an existing surface that can be kept clear and enough discipline to avoid overlapping labeling tasks. It assumes label cross-assignment is a meaningful source of errors; it will not reliably catch an incorrect identifier already printed consistently across all source documents. Frequent interruptions may reduce throughput. Reversal simply restores the previous preparation sequence while retaining all completed tracking and correction records.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Over two weeks, use a predetermined alternating schedule of ordinary preparation and one-sample preparation, with equal coverage of each technician where feasible. Keep receiving checks and end-of-batch audits identical. Record confirmed wrong-label events per sample, handoff seconds and daily unresolved mismatches with their age; also record preparation time to expose any shifted workload. Rehearse with spare paper identifiers to inspect whether an interruption leaves an unambiguous active sample and label. The proposal is weakened if multiple samples accumulate in the active area, label errors remain unchanged, or preparation delays grow without an observable reduction in mismatches. Treat a zero-error fortnight as limited evidence, not proof.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Keep one technician responsible from intake to completion
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Replace routine transfers of partly processed samples with end-to-end responsibility. Assign each incoming sample to one of the two technicians in the shared spreadsheet; that technician performs its processing and closes its record. Both technicians continue working, but divide samples rather than dividing processing stages. The mechanism is reducing the number of custody changes where a sample can become associated with another sample's label or spreadsheet row.

First inspect the intake forms and last month's correction log to identify a processing route both technicians can complete. Apply ownership to that route, balancing assignments by expected workload rather than assuming every sample takes equal effort. Shared equipment can still be scheduled between technicians without transferring sample responsibility. Preserve all printed labels and original identifiers. Record owner, processing status and any unavoidable transfer in the existing spreadsheet, with one editor at a time.

For an unexpected mismatch, pause that sample, retain its label and intake documentation, and record conflicting identifiers verbatim. Resolve only from documentary evidence, appending the correction and its basis without deleting the original record. Never relabel from memory. If an owner becomes unavailable, record an explicit exception transfer rather than allowing unrecorded substitution.

This requires both technicians to be qualified for the selected route and equipment scheduling that permits individual responsibility. It may worsen queues where specialization is essential, and it cannot prevent mistakes already present at intake. Reversal restores stage-based assignments while retaining ownership and correction records.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For two weeks, assign comparable eligible batches by a predetermined alternating sequence to individual ownership or current stage-based handling. Give both groups the same final comparison against intake records. Record confirmed wrong-label counts and sample denominators, total handoff seconds per batch, seconds per actual handoff, and daily unresolved mismatch counts and ages. Record completion time to expose displaced delays. A batch with no transfer has zero total handoff time; its per-handoff time is not applicable. Inspect the first day's records: if ownership does not reduce actual transfers, its mechanism has failed. Revise or reject it if errors persist or queues materially worsen. Low error counts will leave effectiveness uncertain.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Spreadsheet reconciliation that exposes duplicate and missing identifiers
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use the shared spreadsheet to flag impossible or incomplete handoff records automatically. The mechanism is a consistency check across the whole batch: assigning the same identifier to two containers should also leave another expected identifier missing. This can expose errors that remain unnoticed when technicians inspect samples individually.

Create a trial tab containing the expected identifiers from existing intake forms, preserving the original records. For each handoff, the receiving technician enters the identifier actually visible on each container into a separate observed column, formatted as text to preserve leading zeros. Use ordinary spreadsheet formulas or conditional formatting to flag unexpected identifiers, repeated identifiers and expected samples without a receipt. Do not populate observed identifiers automatically from the expected list. Process one editor at a time.

First establish whether identifiers uniquely identify containers. Where legitimate derivatives share a parent identifier, reconcile their documented container identifiers or expected multiplicities separately; do not invent replacement identities. Keep original labels intact. Hold flagged samples with their intake documentation, record conflicting values verbatim, and append evidence-backed resolutions without overwriting the original observation. Never relabel from memory.

This requires spreadsheet functions already available and time to enter observed identifiers. It assumes duplicate, omitted or unexpected identifiers explain some errors in last month's correction log. A complete swap between two valid identifiers will pass reconciliation, and typing mistakes can create false alarms. Reversal consists of disabling the trial checks while retaining the observations and correction history.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
First test the formulas on copied historical or fictional rows containing a duplicate, an omission and an unexpected identifier; also include a valid two-sample swap to demonstrate the limitation. Do not alter live labels.

Across two weeks, alternate comparable batches between reconciliation and ordinary recording. Apply the same final intake-document audit to both. Record confirmed wrong-label counts and sample totals, handoff seconds including data entry, and daily unresolved mismatch counts and ages. Distinguish transcription alarms from physical label errors. Inspect whether flags appear before samples advance. Frequent false alarms, ignored flags or unchanged audited errors would challenge usefulness; few errors would leave effectiveness uncertain.

EXPAND.title: Keep custody with one technician through completion
EXPAND.proposal:
Reduce opportunities for handoff errors by assigning each incoming sample to one technician from intake through testing and result entry wherever the workflow permits. Divide the daily 40 samples according to expected workload. Each owner checks the printed label against the original intake form, records ownership in the shared spreadsheet and keeps responsibility through completion. Share equipment by scheduling access rather than transferring sample custody solely to balance the queue.

For a necessary transfer, record the original identifier, outgoing owner, incoming owner and unfinished operation. The receiver checks the label against the intake form before continuing. Preserve original labels and records; hold conflicting samples and document evidence before appending a correction. Never reconstruct identifiers from memory.

The working principle is removing discretionary transfers. The prior source-checked handoff route improves each transfer but assumes the transfer needs to happen. This route could reduce total exposure and coordination time even if the remaining transfers use that same check.

The technicians need overlapping capabilities, access to the relevant equipment and permission to adjust work allocation. Review the correction log to identify avoidable transfers and intake forms to estimate workload. If specialization requires nearly every sample to change hands, this route offers little benefit. Unequal workloads and delayed samples are the main shifted risks. Restore the previous allocation at any time while retaining ownership and correction records.
EXPAND.experiment: Technician A coordinates a two-week trial using a predetermined alternating daily schedule: end-to-end ownership versus the usual division of work with source-checked transfers. Balance sample types where practical. Both technicians record confirmed wrong-label events, total handoff time, unresolved mismatches and their ages daily; also record completed samples and waiting time. Apply the same final source audit in both conditions. First inspect whether any transfers actually disappear. Stop the ownership allocation if it causes samples to miss existing processing deadlines or leaves required work without a qualified owner. Prefer the simple comparator if errors do not decrease and workload or waiting increases. Low error counts will leave effectiveness uncertain.

EXPAND.title: Bind spreadsheet results to an explicit sample key
EXPAND.proposal:
Prevent an accurately labeled sample from becoming associated with the wrong spreadsheet row. At intake, enter the identifier exactly as printed on the original form into a dedicated sample-key column, then check it against the physical label. During result entry and handoff, locate the record by that identifier rather than by row number, current selection or expected order. Confirm that exactly one matching record exists before editing. If identifiers legitimately repeat, use an existing intake-form reference to distinguish records and retain both fields.

Make the working data a single rectangular table and require whole-table sorting; avoid sorting individual columns. Keep original intake fields unchanged during routine processing. Add dated correction entries with the old value, new value, reason and technician rather than silently overwriting identifying information. Use one editor at a time. A missing or duplicate match blocks entry for that sample while unaffected samples continue; preserve the sample and conflicting documents pending documentary resolution.

This changes the digital association mechanism. The prior source-checked handoff can verify an identifier correctly yet still leave a technician entering results into a previously selected row after a sort. This route specifically removes dependence on row position.

Implementation requires only the existing spreadsheet, intake forms and a short agreed editing rule. Review the correction log for row shifts or results posted to neighboring records. It assumes identifiers can distinguish records using existing documentation; it cannot establish which physical sample is correct when source documents conflict. Reversal restores the old navigation method while retaining the audit history.
EXPAND.experiment: Technician B owns a two-week trial, alternating predetermined comparable batches between key-based navigation and the prior source-checked handoff procedure. Use identical final audits, counting physical wrong labels and wrong-record associations separately. Record handoff seconds, daily unresolved mismatches and lookup time. Before live use, try reordered and duplicate records in a paper mock-up to see whether the rule prevents an ambiguous entry. Stop and inspect immediately if a partial-column sort separates identifiers from results. Reject the change if association errors persist or lookup delays exceed any observed benefit. Report counts rather than claiming statistical certainty.

EXPAND.title: Control duplicate and obsolete printed labels
EXPAND.proposal:
Prevent an obsolete but plausible printed label from re-entering use. At the start of each intake group, reconcile available printed labels against the intake forms. Record the expected identifier and number of labels required for each sample, including separately documented derivatives where applicable. Keep unused labels with their corresponding intake paperwork until needed.

Treat every replacement print as an exception: record the identifier, reason and number printed in the shared spreadsheet. If the discarded label is loose, mark it void and retain it with the intake paperwork. If it remains attached to a sample, preserve it and document the correction beside it without obscuring the original identifier. When an expected label cannot be accounted for, hold that sample's labeling or transfer until documentary evidence resolves the discrepancy. Other reconciled samples may continue. At handoff, the receiver sees the exception record for any affected sample.

The mechanism is controlling competing versions and surplus labels. The prior one-sample labeling gate separates simultaneous work, but a technician could still apply an old label to the single active sample. This route targets stale labels left after reprints, cancellations or interrupted intake.

The two technicians need a shared rule for authorized reprints and space with existing paperwork to retain void labels. It adds no barcode system or purchase. Review last month's corrections for duplicate, obsolete or replacement-label incidents before selecting the trial step. It offers little benefit if labels are never reprinted or retained between batches. Accounting can itself become burdensome, and a reconciled count does not prove a label was applied correctly. Reversal removes the accounting requirement while retaining exception history.
EXPAND.experiment: Technician A owns a two-week alternating-batch comparison with the prior one-sample labeling gate. Keep source checks and final audits identical. Record confirmed wrong labels, handoff time and unresolved mismatches daily, plus reconciliation minutes and replacement-print counts. Rehearse with paper labels that include one obsolete duplicate; inspect whether it is removed from use without changing any live identifier. Stop if label accounting causes an existing processing deadline to be missed, and retain source checks during recovery. Prefer the simpler gate if obsolete labels are absent or added accounting produces no observable improvement. A fortnight with no replacement events cannot meaningfully test this mechanism.

EXPAND.title: Require a documented restart after interruptions
EXPAND.proposal:
Reduce errors caused by resuming at an assumed place after an interruption. Define a small set of actual processing stages using the current workflow, such as intake checked, preparation complete and ready for transfer. For each sample, record the last completed stage in the shared spreadsheet only after finishing it. Keep the original intake form available as the source reference.

If a technician is interrupted while handling labels or transferring a sample, the sample remains pending. Before resuming, the technician rereads the physical identifier and intake form, checks the recorded completed stage and re-establishes the next unfinished action. Never interpret a partly completed operation as complete from memory. A relieving technician follows the same restart procedure. If the physical state cannot be reconciled with the record, hold the sample, record the conflicting evidence and resolve from documentation before continuing. Unaffected samples remain available for work.

This changes how work resumes after attention or custody is broken. The prior one-sample gate reduces cross-assignment, but a single active sample can still receive a repeated label operation or an unchecked transfer after interruption. The prior acceptance check does not necessarily reconstruct unfinished processing.

Implementation requires agreed stage definitions and a few spreadsheet fields, with one editor at a time. The correction log can indicate whether interruptions are a plausible contributor, though it may not record them. The main risks are stale stage entries and excessive recording. Stage records do not replace identifier checks. The procedure is reversible by retiring the restart fields while preserving completed records.
EXPAND.experiment: Technician B owns a two-week trial comparing predetermined half-days with the restart rule against the prior one-sample gate, balancing both technicians where possible. Do not deliberately interrupt live critical operations. First use a paper rehearsal interrupted midway through a labeling step and inspect whether either technician can resume without guessing. During live work, record confirmed wrong labels, handoff time and daily unresolved mismatches, plus observed interruptions and restart time. Keep final source audits identical. Stop if stage records repeatedly disagree with physical progress or restart delays threaten existing processing deadlines. If interruptions are rare, or additional recording shifts mistakes into stale status entries, the simpler comparator may be preferable; the trial cannot establish benefit without relevant interruption exposure.

EXPAND.title: Source-checked acceptance with explicit custody recovery
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade the source-checked handoff route by closing its interruption gap: presenting a sample does not transfer responsibility. The sender remains responsible until the receiver completes the source check and records acceptance. If either technician is interrupted before acceptance, the transfer remains pending and the receiver restarts the identifier check before processing. This prevents a partially checked transfer from being treated as complete.

For each transfer, the receiver independently compares the physical label, original intake form and spreadsheet record. Record sender, receiver, acceptance time and accepted or mismatch-pending status, using one spreadsheet editor at a time. The sender keeps pending samples with their forms in a designated existing hold space. After interruption, check the acceptance record before moving or processing the sample; an unclear record requires reconciliation between both technicians, not an assumed transfer.

For conflicting identifiers, retain the original sample, label and paperwork, record the conflicting values verbatim and hold the affected sample. The sender coordinates documentary reconciliation; the receiver checks the supporting evidence before work resumes. Append corrections with their evidence and authors rather than overwriting identifying history. If the available records cannot establish identity, leave the mismatch unresolved.

Both technicians own implementation. It requires only existing forms, the shared spreadsheet and a brief overlap. Review last month's correction log to choose the initial handoff. Compared with the original acceptance procedure, the additional action is limited to interrupted or ambiguous transfers. It may reduce custody gaps but can increase waiting. If reliable overlap is unavailable, retain custody with the sender and defer that transfer rather than waive acceptance. Matching mistakes already present in the source documents remain a limitation. Rollback removes the new custody convention while retaining all acceptance and correction records.
EXPAND.experiment:
Run a two-week trial at one existing handoff, with Technician A compiling daily measurements and both technicians following the procedure. Use predetermined alternating half-days of the original source-checked acceptance procedure and the upgraded procedure, applying identical mismatch containment and final source audits. Record confirmed wrong-label events and samples handled, active handoff seconds, waiting time, and unresolved mismatches with their ages at each day's end. Count each confirmed error once.

Before live use, rehearse an interrupted transfer using paper examples: stop before acceptance and inspect whether both technicians identify the same responsible sender and restart the check. Do not deliberately mislabel live samples. Stop the upgraded transfer arrangement if ambiguous custody leads to processing before acceptance or waiting threatens an existing processing deadline; reconcile affected samples and return to the original procedure with documented custody. Compare error counts and waiting burden, and report uncertainty if few errors or interruptions occur.

EXPAND.title: Remove avoidable container changes before handoff
EXPAND.proposal:
Use physical identity continuity: eliminate a container change performed solely for staging or handoff when the existing laboratory method already permits the sample to remain in its original labeled container. Every avoided transfer removes an opportunity to put soil into a differently labeled container. This differs from checking transfers, assigning fixed positions or restricting labeling to one sample at a time: it removes a label-to-material association step.

Before the trial, both technicians walk through the current process using intake forms and last month's correction log. Identify any container change that is administrative rather than required for testing, preservation, contamination control, capacity or an independently identified aliquot. Apply the procedure only where existing method requirements clearly allow the original container. Do not change analytical methods or assume a container is suitable. If no eligible change exists, do not introduce this route.

For eligible samples, keep the original label visible and transfer the original container with its intake form. Record the original identifier, current custodian and the omitted staging step in the shared spreadsheet. The receiver compares the label with the form and spreadsheet before recording acceptance; until then the sender retains responsibility. If interrupted, retain pending custody and repeat the check on resumption. Required derivatives continue to receive documented parent-to-derivative identifiers under the current procedure.

Hold any identifier conflict with its original evidence. Resolve only from documentation, append corrections and leave unsupported identity unresolved. If retaining the container obstructs a required operation, revert to the existing documented container-transfer procedure before that operation. Both technicians own this decision within their existing work responsibilities. No new equipment is required. Compared with ordinary recontainerization, this could reduce handling and label work, but may shift inconvenience to equipment access or staging. Its usefulness depends on an avoidable container change actually existing. Rollback restores that change while retaining traceability records.
EXPAND.experiment:
First inspect one day's workflow and stop this route before live testing if neither technician can identify a clearly method-compatible, avoidable container change. If eligible work exists, Technician B coordinates a two-week trial, alternating comparable eligible batches between original-container handling and current container handling. Keep source checks, mismatch containment and final audits identical.

Measure confirmed wrong-label events per sample, handoff seconds and daily unresolved mismatches with their ages. Also record container changes avoided, total handling time and any staging or equipment delays. Inspect the first eligible batch before its next required operation to confirm that original-container use remains compatible. Stop for any conflict with existing method requirements, contamination controls or processing deadlines; return affected samples to the documented standard process with identifiers checked against source records. Report eligible sample counts separately: a small eligible subset or no observed errors cannot establish a general reduction in mislabeling.
